extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, research integrity professionals, and readers interested in retractions and publication ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying plagiarism and related indicators (copied titles/figures, sentence-level similarity, 'tortured phrases') in submitted or published journal articles and deciding corrective actions such as retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and figures copied from prior article
rubrics_metrics.description: The title and figures have been taken directly from a 2005 article published in Lancet: https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(05)67725-2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct reuse of a prior article's title and figures constitutes plagiarism and is grounds for retraction; the retraction notice explicitly cites direct taking of title and figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-by-sentence similarity to prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: The article appears to follow the Lancet article on a sentence-by-sentence basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High degree of sequential similarity (not just shared ideas) is a strong indicator of copying; reviewers/editors should look for structural and phrasing parallels beyond isolated shared facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of 'tortured phrases' as evidence of problematic generation/paraphrase
rubrics_metrics.description: The wording 'follows the Lancet one on a sentence-by-sentence level while using tortured phrases' — tortured phrases are what happens to words that get translated from English into a foreign language, then back to English — perhaps by a computer trying to generate a scholarly publication for a group of unscrupulous authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Odd, unnatural phrasings ('tortured phrases') can indicate back-translation, automated generation, or paper-mill output and should prompt closer scrutiny for underlying plagiarism or fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of plagiarism checks at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal regrets that these issues were not identified during the plagiarism check at the time of submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should run robust plagiarism screening at submission; failure of screening to detect substantial copying is a lapse in editorial process and may require process improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction is appropriate when evidence supports copying and editors/authors agree
rubrics_metrics.description: This article has been retracted by the Editor-in-Chief. ... The authors agree with this decision to retract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When clear evidence of copying exists (e.g., direct reuse of title/figures and sentence-level similarity) and the editorial office determines misconduct or unacceptable overlap, retraction is an appropriate corrective action; author agreement may accompany the notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of anonymous tips and watchdog reporting in post-publication detection
rubrics_metrics.description: An anonymous tipster informed Retraction Watch of the issue; Retraction Watch raised questions which preceded the retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication scrutiny by readers, anonymous whistleblowers, and watchdog outlets can surface problems that initial review missed; journals should have channels to receive and investigate such reports.
